title: Arete Capital Dedicated capacity discovery
summary: Discovery focused on dedicated GPU capacity, isolation requirements, burst strategy and autoscaling expectations. Customer wants predictable throughput for inference pipelines with strict data controls and SOC2-level auditability. SE provided architecture options (Dedicated + VPC) and discussed burst to hosted tier, KV caching, batching, and quantization tradeoffs.

Priya to schedule 1-hr technical deep dive for model benchmark (endpoints + sample prompts)
Customer to share expected qps and sample prompt set for benchmarking

transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Arete), Maria (Arete), Omar (Arete)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we wanted to cover your dedicated capacity needs and make sure we capture isolation requirements and burst strategy, so I'll hand it over to Liam for context on what you're running today.

[00:18] Liam: Yeah thanks Jordan. So quick context, we run a few inference pipelines for risk models and document processing, roughly 600 rps at peak across a mix of short prompts and long-context summarization. We're evaluating dedicated GPUs because of data isolation and consistent latency SLOs.

[00:38] Maria: And to add, we have strict regulatory constraints — some workloads must stay in a private VPC and we need audit logs and KMS integration.

[00:50] Priya: Got it. When you say 600 rps is that concurrent requests or token-level throughput? Like, are those small prompt calls or streaming long runs?

[01:05] Liam: It's requests per second; most are small (under 2k tokens) but about 20% are longer summarizations that go up to 8k tokens. 99th percentile latency target is sub-400ms for the small ones.

[01:26] Omar: For security we need SOC2 and ISO readiness, SSO via SAML, and KMS/HSM for key management. We also need the option to run in an on-prem or VPC private control plane later.

[01:42] Jordan: That's common — Redwood Dedicated supports VPC private deployments and we have an on-prem package for air-gapped needs. We'll make sure to include compliance docs.

[02:00] Priya: From a capacity perspective, two major questions: 1) what GPU profile gives you predictable latency for the mix you described, and 2) how do you want to handle bursts — pure reserved capacity or a hybrid where you can overflow to hosted?

[02:18] Maria: Hybrid would be ideal. We want predictable baseline capacity for business-critical flows but ability to burst for seasonal peaks without long procurement cycles.

[02:30] Priya: Great. For predictable latency you'd usually reserve an N-card pool. For example, 8x A100 or 16x A10 equivalent depending on model size and quantization. We recommend test runs — profiling your actual models on our dedicated machines — because kernel selection, kv-cache behavior, and token lengths drive throughput.

[02:56] Liam: Can you explain kv-cache and how that helps with the long context summaries? I heard about it but not fully sure.

[03:08] Priya: Yeah, kv-cache stores compiled key/value states between tokens for an in-progress generation which reduces recompute for long sequences. For chat-style or streaming cases, it improves latency and reduces GPU memory churn. BUT if you have many short independent requests, batching helps more. So the workload shape matters — and that determines the GPU counts.

[03:36] [04:00] Maria: What about autoscaling? We need both vertical and horizontal scaling options without violating data isolation.

[04:12] Jordan: Dedicated gives you reserved horizontal pools. You can configure autoscale policies within the pool (scale by queue depth, p99 latency, or scheduled events). For privacy, autoscale stays within your reserved fleet. For bursts beyond reserved capacity you can configure overflow to Redwood hosted endpoints but only for workloads you opt-in — and for PII/data-sensitive jobs we'd recommend not enabling overflow or using token redaction/cached responses.

[04:50] Omar: Overflow to hosted raises data residency alarms. If we use overflow we'd need to ensure data is anonymized or explicitly allowed. Also want guarantees around logging and audit trails when overflow occurs.

[05:06] Priya: We can attach labels to requests and produce audit logs showing which routing policy handled the request, timestamp, and model variant. We'll include an example in the security pack.

[05:22] Liam: On performance, what's the expected latency improvement from quantization? We were considering int8 or 4-bit for cost savings.

[05:32] Priya: Quantization can reduce GPU memory and improve throughput, but may add a small quality delta. For retrieval-augmented generation we usually recommend 8-bit or mixed precision first, evaluate quality, then move to int8/4-bit for cost-sensitive batch workloads. We'll include model-specific recommendations after bench marking.

[05:52] Jordan: Also important: caching and batching strategies can reduce per-token cost substantially. For example, prefix caching for repeated system prompts and a small request-level cache for common queries. That can change the sizing math.

[06:08] Maria: Good point. Our most expensive paths are the long summarization jobs that are less cacheable.

[06:18] Priya: For those we might allocate larger sequence-optimized instances — and use preemptible/burst nodes for batch-only runs if you want cost savings during off-peak. But note preemptible means less predictable availability.

[06:34] Omar: On encryption: we need KMS integration and audit logs with the key IDs. Can Redwood support customer-managed keys?

[06:43] Jordan: Yes, Redwood supports CMK with integrations to AWS KMS and HSM options for Private deployments. We'll surface how keys are used in the control plane and in-flight encryption details.

[07:00] Liam: We'd like to run a POC. What's the scope you recommend? We're thinking 2-4 week POC with a) baseline perf numbers on our sample prompts, b) security review, and c) SLO verification.

[07:15] Priya: That sounds right. Typical POC: provision a small dedicated pool (e.g., 4x A10s), run your core models with sample prompt set, collect latency/throughput + p99, then iterate on batch sizes/quantization and caching. We'll also test burst to hosted if you want to validate overflow.

[07:34] Maria: Timeline wise we want to decide within four weeks and start a pilot in September. Procurement will need pricing and SLA details.

[07:45] Jordan: We'll send dedicated pricing and a baseline performance spreadsheet today or tomorrow, and Priya will follow up with a detailed benchmark runbook and request list.

[08:00] Omar: One more on compliance: we need SOC2 Type II evidence and any penetration test reports. Also questions on vendor onboarding — can you provide an attestation for data residency controls?

[08:16] Jordan: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 artifacts and our security pack. For vendor attestation we can provide a summary of controls and a contact for legal to run through the onboarding questionnaire.

[08:30] Liam: Ok sounds good. A couple of clarifying Qs: what is your typical lead time to add more GPUs to a dedicated pool, and what does the billing look like for reserved vs burst?

[08:45] Priya: Lead time is usually a few business days to scale within an existing pool if we have capacity. For new pool procurement it can be longer but we often have reserved inventory. Billing: reserved capacity is a monthly commit; burst to hosted is usage-billed (per-token). We'll put sample math in the pricing sheet.

[09:05] Maria: Are there any networking constraints — do you require specific egress IPs, or can we bring our own NAT?

[09:13] Priya: For VPC/private deployments you control the egress/NAT. For Redwood-managed dedicated in a cloud region we can provide static egress or IP ranges for firewall allow-listing.

[09:28] Omar: Good. Also need RBAC integration with our identity provider and SAML provisioning.

[09:35] Jordan: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning for users, and role-based access controls. We'll include an example RBAC matrix.

[09:46] Liam: Anything else we should be aware of?

[09:50] Priya: Just that the model variant lifecycle matters — pinning a model version for a reserved fleet avoids unexpected perf changes. We support rollouts and automatic fallback to older variants if a new model degrades.

[10:08] Jordan: Great so to recap: Redwood will send pricing + perf spreadsheet, Priya will send benchmark runbook, Arete will share sample prompts + p99 targets, and Oman — sorry Omar — will share compliance questionnaire items and specifics on KMS. We'll aim to reconvene for the technical deep dive week of 2026-08-16.

[10:34] Maria: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[10:38] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with attachments.

End of transcript.
